Do not strain, and skip or release any area that causes significant discomfort. Did I practise without pain or straining? Which areas felt tense, and did I notice any difference after releasing them? mind-resilience Mind & Resilience mood-wellbeing Mood & Wellbeing

items.title: Try Quiet Wakeful Rest After Learning
items.search_text: Try Quiet Wakeful Rest After Learning After learning material you want to remember, try a short period of quiet, minimally stimulating wakeful rest before switching to another demanding task. Treat it as a personal experiment, not a guaranteed memory boost or a universal ten-minute rule. When you finish a focused learning episode, put aside the material and spend a brief period awake in a quiet, low-stimulation setting. Avoid immediately switching to social media, problem solving, reading new material, or another cognitively demanding task. Choose a duration that is practical for you, then return to normal activity. What did I learn, did I actually create a low-interference pause afterward, and when I checked later did recall seem better, unchanged, or worse than usual? learning-thinking Learning & Thinking memory Memory

items.title: Try Short High-Intensity Intervals Safely
items.search_text: Try Short High-Intensity Intervals Safely Perform a HIIT session with 20 seconds of intense exercise (like sprinting or jumping jacks) followed by 10 seconds of rest, repeated for 8 rounds. If vigorous exercise is appropriate for your current fitness and health, choose a simple movement you can perform safely and try a short interval session at an intensity you can control. Treat 20 seconds of work and 10 seconds of rest as one possible interval format, not a universal prescription, and stop if you feel pain or become unwell. Was this level of intensity appropriate for me today, did I keep good control of the movement, and did I have any pain, dizziness, unusual breathlessness or other reason to stop? health-energy Health & Energy fitness-strength Fitness & Strength

items.title: Use a High-Intensity Interval Timer Safely
items.search_text: Use a High-Intensity Interval Timer Safely Follow the Tabata protocol: 20 seconds of very intense exercise (like burpees or mountain climbers) followed by 10 seconds of rest, repeated for 4 minutes (8 rounds). If very vigorous exercise is suitable for you, use an interval timer to alternate a short period of harder work with recovery. A 20-second work and 10-second recovery pattern can be one option, but choose a movement and number of rounds you can control safely rather than treating 8 all-out rounds as mandatory. items.title: Use a Short Phrase to Choose the Next Step
items.search_text: Use a Short Phrase to Choose the Next Step Use a brief phrase as a cue to acknowledge a difficult moment and choose one small, controllable action. The phrase is a reminder, not a prediction about how the situation will end. When you feel stuck, pause and repeat a short phrase once. Name what is difficult in plain language, then choose one action that is small enough to begin now. Skip the phrase if it feels hollow, pressuring or unrelated to the real problem. What was difficult, what action did I choose, and did the phrase help me begin or should I use a different cue next time? focus-action Focus & Action task-initiation Task Initiation

items.title: Use a Short Timebox for a Rough First Pass
items.search_text: Use a Short Timebox for a Rough First Pass Give a low-risk task a shorter-than-usual timebox, define what a useful first pass must contain, and reduce scope instead of pretending you can preserve everything by working faster. Pick a low-risk task where an imperfect first pass is useful. Set a short timebox, define the minimum useful output, and decide what you will leave for later. Stop or reassess when the timebox ends. Did the timebox help me make useful scope decisions, and what should be improved before this work is actually finished or shared? creativity-expression Creativity & Expression idea-generation Idea Generation

items.title: Use Active Recall for Retention, Then Practice Application
items.search_text: Use Active Recall for Retention, Then Practice Application Try to retrieve what you learned without looking, check the answer, and correct errors. Use active recall when retention matters; if the real goal is applying a rule or performing a skill, add separate application practice instead of assuming better recall will transfer automatically. Choose a small set of material you want to retain. Put the source out of view and answer questions or explain the material from memory. Then compare your response with the source, correct mistakes, and note what you could not retrieve. If success ultimately means solving, writing, speaking, calculating, or performing, add a separate task that practices that application. Could I retrieve the target information without looking? What did I get wrong? If my goal involves application, could I actually use the rule or knowledge in a relevant task? learning-thinking Learning & Thinking memory Memory skill-learning Skill Learning

items.title: Use an Extreme Seed, Then Return to Reality
items.search_text: Use an Extreme Seed, Then Return to Reality Start an idea session with a deliberately unrealistic seed, explore its consequences without defending it and then translate useful fragments back into real constraints. State the real problem. Choose an extreme seed that changes one constraint, customer, resource or rule. During a short generation round, list consequences and variants without arguing with the seed. Remove the seed, restore actual constraints and choose one feasible fragment to test or develop. items.title: Use the 20-20-20 Rule for Screen Breaks
items.search_text: Use the 20-20-20 Rule for Screen Breaks When you spend a long time looking at screens, take a short distance-viewing break: about every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet away for 20 seconds. During long periods of screen use, take a short visual break about every 20 minutes and look at something about 20 feet away for 20 seconds. Use the reminder as a simple screen-rest cue, not as a treatment or a substitute for eye care. items.title: Use WOOP to Turn a Wish Into an If-Then Plan
items.search_text: Use WOOP to Turn a Wish Into an If-Then Plan Use a Wish, desired Outcome, likely internal Obstacle, and a concrete if-then Plan to make one meaningful goal easier to act on. Treat the method as a self-regulation tool, not a guarantee of goal achievement. Choose one meaningful and reasonably feasible wish. Describe the outcome you want, identify an internal obstacle that could derail you, then write: If I notice this obstacle, then I will take this specific action. Try the plan in real life and revise it if the cue or response is not useful. Did the obstacle actually appear, did my if-then response help me act, and what should I keep or change next time? focus-action Focus & Action goals Goals

items.title: Use Your Senses to Return to the Present
items.search_text: Use Your Senses to Return to the Present Spend 3–5 minutes focusing on your senses. Notice what you see, hear, smell, feel, and taste. Gently redirect your attention whenever your mind wanders. Pause somewhere safe and deliberately notice what is happening around you right now. Choose a few sights, sounds, textures, smells or tastes and describe them simply. When your attention drifts into planning, worry or commentary, notice that and gently return to one sensory detail.
